appraisal_events.evidence: 'Morel accusait M. de Charlus de sa tristesse, sans pouvoir fournir d'explications, l'insultait de sa méfiance, à l'aide de raisonnements faux... le menaçait de résolutions désespérées, au milieu desquelles persistait le souci le plus retors de l'intérêt le plus immédiat.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator, pitying Charlus, portrays Morel as unstable and manipulative, hurling baseless accusations and threats at Charlus while calculating his own advantage underneath.

appraisal_events.evidence: 'Il vivait si simplement qu'on ne soupçonnait pas à quel point il était riche'... 'personne ne fut jamais si généreux', especially toward poor young women 'honteuses de recevoir tant pour si peu de chose.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator paints an admiring portrait of Bergotte as unpretentious despite great wealth, remarkably generous, and disdainful of fashionable society.

appraisal_events.evidence: Before Vermeer's little patch of yellow wall: 'C'est ainsi que j'aurais dû écrire... Mes derniers livres sont trop secs, il aurait fallu passer plusieurs couches de couleur, rendre ma phrase en elle-même précieuse.'
appraisal_events.explanation: In his final moments, dying before the Vermeer, Bergotte judges his own late work harshly against the painting's precious density of detail, regretting that his late books fall short.

status_effects.explanation: Morel is exposed as unstable and abusive toward Charlus, combining baseless accusation and threat with calculated self-interest.
Charlus is cast as a pitiable victim who bound his life to an unstable, accusatory partner without knowing it at the start.
Bergotte is admiringly elevated by the narrator as unpretentious and exceptionally generous despite great and unsuspected wealth.
In a separate, later moment, Bergotte's own dying verdict on his late work as insufficiently 'precious' compared to Vermeer's mastery locally diminishes his self-assessment as a writer.
